answer: Next hop data is modelled under the RIB because each entry in 'show next-hop' represents a RIB identified by the 'name' key, and all routes in a RIB belong to the same address family. For each routing instance the system provides one system-controlled default RIB per supported address family, so the RIB is what ties a next hop to an instance and family. Syntax: show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> [next-hop-address]. rib-name is a string of length 1..64 with pattern ([A-Za-z0-9 -.,]*), destination-prefix is an IP prefix, interface is the outgoing interface reference (for example DCN), and next-hop-address is an IPv4 or IPv6 address. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration. Example: show next-hop-IPv4/0.0.0.0/0/DCN.

Use clear [-f] ospf [instance=]<value>. The clear ospf command removes and restarts an ospf-instance, and the operation is asynchronous, so the CLI does not wait for the restart to complete. The instance id is supplied as <instance> and is a string. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation; without it you are prompted to confirm. Access mode is Operational Mode only. Example: clear ospf 1. Note that the ospf-instance command page also points to clear for removing an OSPF instance from the configuration asynchronously.

No. The ospf-area commands are add/set/show/delete ospf-area-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id> [ospf-area-type <value>], and the only permitted value for ospf-area-type is normal, which is also the default. There is no stub or NSSA option. instance-id is uint8 in range 0..255 and ospf-area-id is a dotted-quad. The pre-condition is that the OSPF instance must be created before the area can be added. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add ospf-area-1/0.0.0.0.

Use ospf-area-range, which summarizes routes for an OSPF area matching address/mask, and it is applicable to Area Border Routers (ABRs) only. Syntax: add|set ospf-area-range-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<prefix> [advertise <value>], plus show and delete on the same AID. The prefix may be an IPv4 prefix (length up to 32) or an IPv6 prefix (length up to 128) in canonical form. The advertise parameter takes true or false and defaults to true, where false hides the range. Pre-condition: the OSPF instance must be created before the area can be added. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add ospf-area-range-1/9.9.9.9/10.220.0.0/16 advertise true.

Yes. ospf-instance takes a version parameter with values ospfv2 or ospfv3, defaulting to ospfv2, and version is only settable at add time (add ospf-instance-<instance-id> router-id <value> [version <value>] [description <value>] [router-id-mode <value>]). The router id is controlled by router-id-mode, values manual or use-loopback, default use-loopback; with manual you supply router-id as a dotted-quad. Pre-condition: if router-id-mode is use-loopback then an ipv4 LO-MGMT address must be configured. instance-id is uint8 0..255 and description is a string of length 0..128. Example: add ospf-instance-2 description xyz router-id-mode use-loopback version ospfv3.

On ospf-interface-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name> the defaults are hello-interval 10 seconds (uint16, range 1..32767) and router-dead-interval 40 seconds (uint16, range 4..65535). Related defaults: retransmission-interval 5 seconds (2..3600), transmit-delay 1 second (1..450), ospf-cost 10 (1..65535), priority 1 (0..255), enable true, ospf-if-routing auto (active, passive, auto). Authentication is available: ospf-auth-enable is true/false, default false, and is only of relevance for ospfv2 or ospfv3; ospf-auth-algorithm is none or HMAC_SHA_256, default HMAC_SHA_256, and ospf-auth-key is an ASCII string of length 0..256, both only of relevance for ospfv2. Pre-condition: the OSPF instance and OSPF area must be present.

Use show ospf-neighbor-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>/<router-id> [state] [role] [address] [priority]. The state values are: down (initial state, no Hello packets received from the neighbor), init (Hellos received but bidirectional communication not yet established), 2-way (bidirectional communication established, DR/BDR election occurs here), exstart (DR and BDR elected, master-slave relation determined), exchange (neighbors exchange DataBaseDescriptor (DBD) packets containing LSA headers), loading (routers exchange full Link State information based on DBDs), and full (full adjacency achieved). The role values are drother (Designated Router Other), dr (Designated Router), bdr (Backup Designated Router) and ptp (point-to-point). Access mode is Operational Mode. An OSPF neighbor is deleted when the OSPF interface is down.

Use ospfv3-ipsec-security-association: add ospfv3-ipsec-security-association-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>/<spi> integrity-algorithm <value> [ipsec-protocol <value>] [ipsec-mode <value>], with matching set, show and delete. The integrity-algorithm values are AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_256_128, AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_384_192, AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_512_256, AUTH_HMAC_SHA1_160 and AUTH_HMAC_SHA1_96; it is mandatory on add and has no default. ipsec-protocol indicates ESP or AH but only ESP is offered, default ESP; ipsec-mode supports only transport, default transport. spi is a unique uint32 in range 256..4294967295. Pre-condition: the OSPF instance must be created first. Example: add ospfv3-ipsec-security-association-1/0.0.0.0/DCN/256 integrity-algorithm AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_256_128.

Use ping [-c=<count>] [-w=<timeout>] [-s=<pktsize>] [-i=<interface> | -v=<vrf>] <ping-dest>. -i=<interface> specifies the source interface; by default the interface is selected according to the routing table. -v=<vrf> specifies the VRF; by default the MGMT VRF is used. The interface and VRF name parameters are mutually exclusive. -c stops after sending count ECHO_REQUEST packets, -w sets a timeout in seconds before ping exits regardless of packets sent or received, and -s sets the payload octets excluding headers, default 56 plus 8 octets of ICMP header for a total packet size of 64 octets. ping-dest can be an ipv4-address, ipv6-address or domain-name. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration. Example: ping -c=1 -w=10 -s=1024 192.0.2.3.

Use show protocols, which lists all protocol information in one place, then drill into any one with show protocols <name>. The selectable protocols are ssh, cli, serial-console, netconf, restconf, grpc, snmp, http-file-server and data-model-openconfig. Each sub-view shows its own settings, for example ssh (enabled, port 8022, host keys, pre/post-login messages), cli (enabled true, port 22, script-dir /storage/scripts), serial-console (global-switch, global-timeout 60 minutes), netconf (enabled true, port 830), restconf (https-enabled true, http-port 8080, https-port 8181, cookie-timeout 5 minutes, api-root /restconf), grpc (enabled true, port 50051), snmp (enabled true, port 161, snmp-engine-id) and http-file-server (http-port 8980, https-port 8981, url-base /transfer). Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration.

Use show rib-<rib-name> [vrf] [address-family]. Each entry represents a RIB identified by the 'name' key and all routes in a RIB belong to the same address family; for each routing instance the system provides one system-controlled default RIB for each supported address family. rib-name is a string of length 1..64, vrf is a leafref to ../../vrf/name giving the VRF the RIB is bound to, and address-family takes ipv4-unicast or ipv6-unicast. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: show rib-IPv4 views the RIB identified by the 'IPv4' key.

Use show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> [special-next-hop] [source-protocol]. The route command shows the list of system routes from various sources such as dynamic protocols and static route, and source-protocol is the source protocol for the route entry, for example OSPF, BGP or static. special-next-hop indicates any special treatment for IPv4/IPv6 static routes, rib:routes and IP Monitoring: none (no special treatment, used for all normal routes, and the default), blackhole (for blackhole routes no next-hop is created under route) and unreachable (for unreachable routes no next-hop is created under route). rib-name is a string of length 1..64. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: show route.

Yes. show routing displays routing information. It takes no parameters at all, so it is issued exactly as show routing. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For the detailed views, the related commands are show rib-<rib-name> [vrf] [address-family] for the RIB entries per address family, show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> [special-next-hop] [source-protocol] for the system routes and their source protocol, show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> [next-hop-address] for next hops, and show vrf-<name> for the routing instances.

show supporting-interface-<name>/<interface> shows supporting interface information, that is, which underlying interface supports a given interface. The parameters are name, the name of the interface, a string; and interface, a reference to the IPv4/IPv6 interface given as the path ../../../../../networking/interface/if-name. Both are used only in show. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

traceroute follows a maximum of 30 hops by default: -m=<hopcnt> sets the maximum number of hops (max time-to-live value), uint8 in range 1..255, default 30. The VRF defaults to MGMT: -v=<vrf> specifies the VRF to be used and if not provided defaults to MGMT. Syntax: traceroute [-m=<hopcnt>] [-w=<timeout>] [-i=<interface> | -v=<vrf>] <tr-dest> [pktsize]. -w is the timeout in seconds, uint16 range 1..10, default 2. -i=<interface> sets the source interface, otherwise the interface is selected according to the routing table; the interface and VRF name parameters are mutually exclusive. pktsize is the total probe packet size, default 60 (60 bytes for IPv4). Example: traceroute -m=10 -w=3 1.2.3.4.

Use show vrf-<name> [type] [chassis-name] [description], which shows the Virtual Routing and Forwarding (VRF) instance. chassis-name is the associated chassis name for that VRF. name is a string of length 0..32, type is mgmt (Management VRF) or internal (Internal VRF), and description is a string of length 0..255 describing the VRF and its intended purpose. All four parameters are used in show only. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Example: show vrf-MGMT displays the Management VRF attributes.

activate [-f] swimage [label <string>] [db-action <empty-db|upgrade-db|rollback|auto>] activates the currently installable software image, and a successful swimage activation implies a system restart. db-action specifies the expected database operation: auto (the system default behavior, the default value), empty-db (activate with an empty database), upgrade-db (activate by upgrading the current database) and rollback (roll back to the previous active software image). If db-action is not provided the system decides automatically. Unless -f is given, you must confirm the activation when prompted. label specifies the sw image/manifest file name; if not specified the currently installable image is used. Access mode is Operational Mode. Example: activate swimage db-action=empty-db.

No, only a single location led test can be running at a time. Use activate location-led [entity=]<value> [[timeout=]<value>] [[led-mode=]<value>], where entity is a chassis or a card. led-mode is flash (default), an amber light flashing at 1Hz, usually for LED location, or solid, a steady amber light, usually for lamp test; when lamp test is enabled all chassis LEDs light amber. To turn it off, use terminate location-led [entity=]<value>, or set timeout, a number in range 0..120 seconds, default 0, which means no timeout so the function runs until terminated. The timeout parameter does not take effect in 1830 GX G30 R5.1, so use terminate there. Not all cards support the Location LED test. Example: activate location-led card-1-1.

Use bootstrap ([local-port=]<value> | [neighbor-address=]<value>) [new-admin-user=]<value> [new-password=]<value>. It bootstraps a neighbor NE by establishing a TLS connection over the OSC link and provisioning the initial administrator account, for commissioning an OSC peer NE that has no configured users yet. Select the neighbor either with local-port, the supporting-port of a MGMT vrf osc-eth interface (same value as in show interface, e.g. 1-1-dwdm-line1), which the system maps to the OCE netdev OCE-<chassis>-<slot>-<vlan-id> and resolves to the peer IPv6 link-local address via get_osc_neighbors.sh (if resolution fails the RPC is rejected), or with neighbor-address, the IPv6 link-local address including zone, string length 7..256 matching pattern fe80:.*. new-admin-user is mandatory, length 1..32, and follows local user naming rules; new-password may be plain text (standard complexity rules apply) or a $6$ SHA512 hash. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration.

Type cancel-upgrade. The command cancels any active upgrade in progress. Full syntax is cancel-upgrade [-h], where -h is the only flag and displays help for this command; there are no other parameters and no entity or AID to supply. Access mode is Operational mode. Pre-condition: an upgrade must be in progress for this command to execute successfully, so if nothing is running the command will not execute successfully. Example given in the guide: cancel-upgrade, which cancels any active upgrade.

change-ztp-mode enabled starts ZTP, reverts the database to the factory default and triggers a system reboot, so re-enabling it on an in-service node wipes the configuration back to factory defaults and reboots. Syntax: change-ztp-mode [-f] [ztp-mode=]<value>, where ztp-mode takes enabled or disabled and has no default, and -f forces the command without confirmation, so leave -f off to get the confirmation prompt. change-ztp-mode disabled disables ZTP and stops ZTP if it is already in progress; the command can be executed while ZTP is running, interrupting it. The current ZTP mode is displayed with show ztp. Access mode is Operational mode.

Use show current-fw-<card-name>-<port-name>/<fw-name> [fw-version] [expected-fw-version] [fw-status] (variants also accept <card-name>.<slot-name>, <chassis-name>-<slot-name> or <name>). Compare fw-version, the current version of the firmware, against expected-fw-version, the expected version; both are strings of length 0..32. fw-status gives the verdict directly: current (current firmware is up-to-date), not-current (current firmware is not up-to-date against the expected one) and unavailable (information on firmware status is currently unavailable), which is also the default. fw-name is a string of length 0..32. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Examples: show current-fw or show current-fw-1-3/DCO_1.

download supports filetype values crl (a Certificate Revocation List in PEM format), database (a previously uploaded database), file (any file to the file-system), krp (key replacement package), local-certificate (passphrase protected X.509 in PKCS#12, or PKCS#7 if pending-import), peer-certificate (X.509v3 in PKCS#12), script (a CLI script from a remote server), swimage (a manifest file plus all files belonging to a SW image), and trusted-certificate (X.509v3 PKCS#7 Root or Intermediate CA). The system automatically stores the downloaded file in an appropriate place, so no local location is needed; use show transfer to see the default storage directory. Only filetype file accepts destination, which may be omitted (default directory, original name), a file-name, a relative path or an absolute path, and you need write access to it. A downloaded database is stored as a db-instance=temp database, overwriting any existing temp.

Use show downloaded-image-<manifest-file>/<name> [signature], which retrieves information about downloaded image files. manifest-file is the downloaded manifest file and its information, a string of length 0..256; name is the name of the downloaded software image, a string of length 0..256; and signature is the downloaded software image file signature, a string of length 0..1024. All parameters are used in show only. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Issue show downloaded-image to list all downloaded software image files.

show downloads is the command that shows a list of downloads. Its syntax is exactly show downloads and it has no parameters. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For image-specific detail on what was pulled down, use show downloaded-image-<manifest-file>/<name> [signature], which reports the manifest file, the downloaded software image name and its file signature. For a transfer still running, in particular one started asynchronously with download -a, use show transfer-status filetype to see the current state, and show transfer to see the default storage directory.
